rationale: A coherent but largely mechanical stacking of three already-evaluated legs (the winning sources+uses sum plus the inventory leg), and the re-z-scoring of the two flow ratios changes the winner's construction, so any gain will be hard to attribute — worth one run, but it is consolidation rather than new economics.

This is a horizon swap that substitutes one already-tested leg (five-year deployment mix) for another already-tested leg (one-year mix) inside an already-tested composite, i.e. a cosmetic variant whose likely outcome is bracketed by results already in the archive.

The conditioning leg is the published hiring-rate/employment-growth anomaly (Bazdresch-Belo-Lin) with its standard sign, multiplied by the cash-to-price anomaly, so the signal is a product of two known effects rather than a new mechanism — and the "flat headcount preserves optionality" story conflates disciplined restraint with genuine demand decline.

A legitimate financing-free ablation of Signal 1 that would sharpen attribution of slope versus alpha, but the raw bounded mix ratio (sd ≈ 0.3) is added to a unit-variance z-score, so the inventory channel will silently dominate and the "two operating channels" framing overstates the balance actually computed.

The winsorize-before-industry-z fix is a genuine diagnosis-driven repair of the deal-history leg's skew problem, but the claim that the two legs are economically distinct is weak since both are acquisition-intensity measures at different horizons, and the raw-versus-z-scored scale mismatch again lets the legacy leg dominate.

This is the most informative proposal in the set because it takes a sign stance on capacity growth that deliberately opposes the published asset-growth/CMA prior yet is directly motivated by the archive's strongly negative capacity-shrinkage result, so the outcome is diagnostic either way — though the same raw-versus-z-score scale imbalance means the growth leg, not the deployment mix, will drive the spread.
